explanations.explanation: Capernaum it is. John 6:24 says the crowd got into the boats and went to Capernaum to look for Him. A whole crowd climbing into boats just to track Him down. Friend, I've seen less hustle at a free sample tray.

Bethsaida is a fair guess, but it's not the town this verse names. John 6:24 says the crowd went to Capernaum. Bethsaida never comes up in these verses. Next time, trust the boats and follow them to Capernaum.

Joppa doesn't show up anywhere in this passage, friend. The crowd gets into the boats and goes to Capernaum (John 6:24). That's the whole trip. Sometimes the answer is the town the verse actually names.

explanations.answer: They ate the loaves and had their fill
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what Jesus says. He tells them, "…you ate the loaves and had your fill." He doesn't even answer the when question. He goes straight to what's really going on. I think that's the kind of honesty only someone who sees the heart can pull off.

explanations.answer: They saw Him walking on the sea
explanations.explanation: Walking on the sea isn't what Jesus brings up here. The crowd only notices that He didn't board the boat with His disciples. What He names is the loaves: "…you ate the loaves and had your fill." He goes right to it.

explanations.answer: They want Him to heal their sick
explanations.explanation: Healing isn't what Jesus names in this verse. He tells them it's "…because you ate the loaves and had your fill." He says it's not because they saw the signs. So the loaves are the reason on the table.

Eternal is the word. Jesus says to work for "…food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you." A cookie on my counter lasts maybe a week if I hide it from myself. This food never runs out.

Earthly sounds close, but Jesus says the opposite direction. He says not to work for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life. That's the food the Son of Man will give. Earthly food is the kind that perishes.
Daily is a nice word, but it isn't what Jesus says. He says food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. Daily food gets eaten and gone. This is the food that lasts.

explanations.answer: To believe in the One He has sent
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, "The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent." They asked about works, plural, and He gives them one. I think that would have surprised me too.

explanations.answer: To keep every command of the law
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, but it's not what Jesus says. He answers, "The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent." The crowd asked what to do, and He points them to believing. So the answer is believing in the One God sent.

explanations.answer: To give to everyone in need
explanations.explanation: Giving is a good thing, but it's not what Jesus names here. He says, "The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent." The crowd asked what work to do, and that's the work He gives. It's believing in the One God sent.
Manna. The crowd says, "Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness…" They're asking Jesus for a bigger sign than the bread they just ate. Now that's a tough crowd.
Figs are a good guess, but the crowd names manna. They say their fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. Then they quote that Scripture about bread from heaven. So it was bread, not fruit.

Honey is a sweet guess, and there's a reason it comes to mind. Exodus 16:31 says manna tasted like wafers made with honey. But the food the crowd names is manna. They say their fathers ate it in the wilderness.

It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says, "…it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven." Moses was Israel's leader, but the Father is the one who gives the bread. Jesus says the true bread comes from Him.

Right. Moses, Israel's leader, is not the giver here. Jesus says, "…it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven." He opens with "Truly, truly," so He wants them to listen.

Hunger is the word. Jesus says, "Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst." He says it right after "I am the bread of life." I've never made a cookie that did that, and I've made a LOT of cookies.
Wander is a nice word, but Jesus doesn't say it here. He says, "Whoever comes to Me will never hunger…" The bread picture goes with hunger and thirst. That's the whole promise in the verse.

Falter doesn't fit this verse, friend. Jesus says whoever comes to Him will never hunger, and whoever believes in Him will never thirst. He just called Himself the bread of life. So hunger is the word that matches.

True. Jesus says, "Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away." If you come, He doesn't send you off. I've been in a place where I thought nobody wanted me, so I know how good that sounds.
It's the opposite, friend. Jesus says, "…the one who comes to Me I will never drive away." Never means never. Whoever comes to Him is not driven away.

Not quite. Jesus says the opposite: "For I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me." So He came for the will of the One who sent Him. That's the verse in a nutshell.

Right. Jesus says, "For I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me." He came to do the will of the One who sent Him. The next verse tells what that will is.

Raise them up. Jesus says the will of the One who sent Him is that He "…shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day." He loses none of them. Keep my ovens warm, because that's something to get ready for.
Judging isn't what Jesus says in this verse. He says He shall lose none of those the Father has given Him, "but raise them up at the last day." So the words here are raising up. That's the promise.

Reward is a fair guess, but Jesus doesn't say it here. He says He will lose none of those the Father gave Him, "but raise them up at the last day." The verse is about raising them up. That's what He does with them.

explanations.answer: They know His father and mother
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. "Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then can He say, 'I have come down from heaven'?" They look at what they know and stop there. I think that's easy to do with someone you've known for a long time.
Tiberias is where those other boats came from (John 6:23), but the grumblers don't mention it. They say, "…whose father and mother we know?" That's what they point to. It's about His family.
That isn't what they say. The grumblers ask, "Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" They point to His father and mother. Followers don't come up in their complaint.

True. Jesus says, "No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day." He says it right after telling them to stop grumbling. The Father is the one doing the drawing.

Jesus actually says it straight. "No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day." The Father who sent Him draws people. So the statement is true.

True. Jesus says no one has seen the Father "…except the One who is from God; only He has seen the Father." That is a big claim about Himself. And it comes right after He quotes the Prophets about being taught by God.

Jesus does say it. The verse reads, "…not that anyone has seen the Father except the One who is from God; only He has seen the Father." So the statement is true. Only the One from God has seen the Father.
Not quite. Jesus says, "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died." The manna was real, and so was the dying. Then He turns to a bread that is different.
Right. Jesus says, "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died." He says it right after calling Himself the bread of life. That sets up the bread that doesn't end in death.
Die is the word. Jesus says, "This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die." Notice the word anyone. That means no special club.

Doubt is an honest word, but it isn't in this verse. Jesus says anyone may eat of the bread from heaven "…and not die." The verse just before it says their fathers ate manna and died. So die is the word that fits.

Sin is a heavy word, and it isn't the one Jesus uses here. He says the bread comes down from heaven "…so that anyone may eat of it and not die." That follows the line about their fathers eating manna and dying. So the word is die.
His flesh. Jesus says, "And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh." He gives it for the life of the world. That's a big thing to say in a synagogue.

Teaching is a good thought, but it isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh." So the bread is His flesh. That's the answer in the verse.

His word is a close cousin of what He says, but it's not the answer. Jesus says, "And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh." He names His flesh. That's what the verse says.

explanations.answer: They have no life in them
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. "Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you." The Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). He said it twice again as "Truly, truly," so He wants them to hear it.

Losing a reward isn't what Jesus says. He says, "…unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you." The Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). So the words are no life in you.

Signs aren't what Jesus talks about in this verse. He says, "…unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you." The Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). The words are no life in you.

explanations.answer: He remains in Jesus and Jesus in him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, "Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in him." Jesus in him and him in Jesus. That's close, friend.

explanations.answer: He sees the Father face to face
explanations.explanation: Seeing the Father isn't what Jesus says here. He says whoever eats His flesh and drinks His blood "…remains in Me, and I in him." Seeing the Father came up earlier, in verse 46, and that was about the One who is from God. This verse is about staying in Jesus.

explanations.answer: He rules the land with Jesus
explanations.explanation: Ruling isn't in this verse. Jesus says whoever eats His flesh and drinks His blood "…remains in Me, and I in him." The picture is closeness, not a throne. Jesus in him and him in Jesus.

Synagogue. John 6:59 says, "Jesus said this while teaching in the synagogue in Capernaum." So all of it happened in a synagogue, not out on the shore. I like to picture the people in the back leaning in.
Temple is a good guess, but the verse says synagogue. John 6:59 says Jesus said this while teaching in the synagogue in Capernaum. That's the place the text gives us.
Marketplace is a lively guess, but it isn't what the verse says. John 6:59 says Jesus said this "…while teaching in the synagogue in Capernaum." So it was a synagogue. The place was Capernaum.
